What is a human but an ingenious machine designed to turn, with
“infinite artfulness, the red wine of Shiraz into urine?” So said the
storyteller in Isak Dinesen’s Seven Gothic Tales. More accurately but
less poetically, human kidneys serve to convert more than 1700 L of
blood per day into about 1 L of a highly concentrated fluid called urine.
In so doing, the kidney excretes the waste products of metabolism;
precisely regulates the body’s concentration of water, salt, calcium,
phosphorus, and other anions and cations; and maintains the appro-
priate acid-base balance of plasma. The kidney also serves as an endo-
crine organ, secreting hormones such as erythropoietin and renin, and
it regulates vitamin D metabolism.
Renal diseases are responsible for a great deal of morbidity and
mortality. According to the 2020 US Renal Data System Annual Data
Report, more than 808,000 Americans had end-stage kidney disease
(ESKD), of whom two-thirds are maintained on dialysis, at a cost of
approximately $72,000 per person annually. The 1-year mortality rate
of ESKD, when the enhanced risk for cardiovascular disease conferred
by ESKD is considered, exceeds that of most newly diagnosed cancers.
Acute kidney injury occurs in more than 2 million people worldwide,
and it is a major risk factor for the development of chronic kidney
disease and ESKD. In addition, millions of people are affected annually
by nonfatal kidney diseases, most notably infections of the kidney
or lower urinary tract, kidney stones, and urinary obstruction. The
availability of dialysis and the success of renal transplantation have
improved the outlook for patients.
The study of kidney diseases is facilitated by categorizing them
according to their primary effects on one of the four basic anatomic
components of the kidney: glomeruli, tubules, interstitium, and
blood vessels. This approach is useful because the early manifestations
of disease primarily affecting one of these components tend to be dis-
tinct. Further, some components seem to be more vulnerable to specific
forms of renal injury; for example, most glomerular diseases are im-
munologically mediated, whereas tubular and interstitial disorders
are frequently caused by toxic or infectious agents. However, some
disorders affect more than one structure, and the anatomic and func-
tional interdependence of the components of the kidney means that
damage to one usually secondarily affects the others. Primary disorders
of the blood vessels, for example, inevitably affect all structures supplied
by these vessels. Severe glomerular damage impairs the flow through
the peritubular vascular system; conversely, tubular destruction, by in-
creasing intraglomerular pressure, induces glomerular injury. Thus,
whatever the origin, all forms of chronic kidney disease ultimately dam-
age all four components of the kidney, culminating in what are called
end-stage kidneys. The functional reserve of the kidney is large, and
much damage may occur before there is evident functional impairment.
For these reasons, recognizing the early signs and symptoms is of high
clinical importance.
CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS OF RENAL DISEASES
The clinical manifestations of renal disease can be grouped into
reasonably well-defined syndromes. Some are unique to glomerular
Malignant Neoplasms, 863
Renal Cell Carcinoma, 863
Urothelial Carcinoma of the Renal Pelvis, 865
diseases, and others are present in diseases that affect any one of the
components.
•  Azotemia is a biochemical abnormality that refers to an elevation
of blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine levels, related largely
to a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Azotemia is a con-
sequence of many renal diseases, but it may also arise from extra-
renal disorders. It is a typical feature of both acute and chronic
kidney injury. Prerenal azotemia is encountered when there is hy-
poperfusion of the kidneys that impairs renal function in the ab-
sence of parenchymal damage. It may be caused by hypotension,
excessive fluid losses from any cause, or if the effective intravascu-
lar volume is decreased due to shock or congestive heart failure.
Postrenal azotemia is seen whenever urine flow is obstructed distal
to the kidney. Relief of the obstruction is followed by correction of
the azotemia.
•  When azotemia leads to clinical signs and symptoms associated
with biochemical abnormalities, it is termed uremia. Uremia is
characterized not only by failure of renal excretory function but
also by a host of metabolic and endocrine alterations resulting from
renal  damage.  Uremic  patients  frequently  manifest  secondary
involvement of the gastrointestinal system (e.g., uremic gastroen-
teritis), peripheral nerves (e.g., peripheral neuropathy), and heart
(e.g., uremic fibrinous pericarditis).
•  Nephritic syndrome is a clinical entity caused by inflammatory
glomerular disease and is dominated by the acute onset of either
grossly visible or microscopic hematuria, diminished GFR, mild
to moderate proteinuria, and hypertension. It is the classic presen-
tation  of  acute  poststreptococcal  glomerulonephritis.  Rapidly
progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is a form of nephritic syn-
drome  in  which  there  is  rapid  decline  in  GFR  (within  hours
to days).
•  Nephrotic syndrome, typically caused by severe dysfunction of the
glomerular filter, is characterized by heavy proteinuria (more than
3.5 g/day), resulting in hypoalbuminemia  and severe edema, and
hyperlipidemia and lipiduria (lipids in the urine).
•  Asymptomatic  hematuria  or  proteinuria,  or  a  combination  of
these two, is usually a manifestation of subtle or mild glomerular
abnormalities.
•  Acute kidney injury (previously called acute renal failure) is char-
acterized by rapid decline in GFR (within hours to days) with
concurrent dysregulation of fluid and electrolyte balance, and re-
tention  of  metabolic  waste  products  normally  excreted  by  the
kidney including urea and creatinine. In its most severe forms, it
is manifested by oliguria or anuria (reduced or no urine flow). It
can result from glomerular, interstitial, vascular, or acute tubular
injury (ATI).
•  Chronic kidney disease (previously called chronic renal failure)
is defined by a diminished GFR that is persistently less than 60
mL/min/1.73 m⁻ for at least 3 months and/or persistent albu-
minuria. It may present with a clinically silent decline in renal
excretory function in milder forms or with prolonged symptoms
and  signs  of  uremia  in  more  severe  cases.  Chronic  kidney

CHAPTER 20  The Kidney 815
KEY CONCEPTS
Clinical Manifestations of Renal Diseases
•  Azotemia is the biochemical manifestation of acute or chronic kidney injury
and is characterized by elevated BUN and serum creatinine. It reflects a
reduction in GFR.
•  Kidney injury that results in azotemia can be either acute or chronic. Acute
kidney injury can be reversible or progress to chronic kidney disease, which
is generally irreversible.
•  One major manifestation of kidney injury is the nephrotic syndrome, in
which injury to the glomerulus results in abnormal filtration, leading to
heavy proteinuria, edema, and metabolic disturbances.
•  Nephritic syndromes are those in which hematuria, azotemia, hypertension,
and subnephrotic proteinuria are the major manifestations.
•  Diseases involving the tubules and interstitium may have clinical manifesta-
tions of the nephritic syndrome, specific defects in tubular function, or acute
or chronic kidney disease without specific defining features.
GLOMERULAR DISEASES
Glomerular  diseases  constitute  some  of  the  major  problems  in
nephrology. Glomeruli may be injured by a variety of factors and in
the course of several systemic diseases. Disorders in which the kidney
is the only or predominant organ involved, such as minimal change
disease or membranous nephropathy, constitute the various types of
primary glomerulonephritis or, because some do not have a cellular
inflammatory component, primary glomerulopathy. Systemic immu-
nologic diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), vascular
disorders such as thrombotic angiopathies, metabolic diseases such as
diabetes mellitus, and some hereditary conditions such as Fabry dis-
ease often affect the glomerulus as one manifestation. These are termed
secondary glomerular diseases. However, both the clinical manifesta-
tions and glomerular histologic changes in primary and secondary
forms can be similar.
In the following sections, we discuss the normal glomerulus and
mechanisms of glomerular injury, and then the various primary glo-
merular diseases. We also briefly review the secondary forms covered in
other parts of this book. Table 20.2 lists the most common forms of
glomerulonephritis that have reasonably well-defined pathologic and
clinical characteristics. The clinical manifestations of glomerular dis-
eases are clustered into the five major groups summarized in Table 20.3.
Both primary glomerular diseases and systemic diseases affecting the
glomerulus can result in these syndromes. Because glomerular diseases
are often associated with systemic disorders, including diabetes, SLE,
vasculitis, and monoclonal paraproteinemias, in any patient with man-
ifestations  of  glomerular  disease,  it  is  essential  to  consider  these
systemic conditions.
Structure of the Glomerulus
Many clinical manifestations of glomerular diseases result from per-
turbations of specific components of the glomerulus, so before dis-
cussing these diseases we describe the key anatomic structures of
glomeruli.  The  glomerulus  consists  of  an  anastomosing  network
of capillaries lined by fenestrated endothelium invested by two layers
of epithelial cells (Fig. 20.1). The visceral epithelial cells, or podocytes,

The glomerular capillary wall is the filtration barrier, and consists
of the following (Fig. 20.2):
•  A thin layer of fenestrated endothelial cells, with each fenestra being
about 70 to 100 nm in diameter.
•  The glomerular basement membrane (GBM) with a thick electron-
dense central layer, the lamina densa, and thinner electron-lucent
peripheral layers, the lamina rara interna and lamina rara externa.
The GBM consists of collagen (mostly type IV), laminin, polyan-
ionic proteoglycans (mostly heparan sulfate), fibronectin, entactin,
and several other glycoproteins. Type IV collagen forms a network
to which other glycoproteins attach. The building block (monomer)
of this network is a triple-helical molecule composed of one or
more of six types of a chains (COL4A1 to COL4A6). Each mole-
cule consists of an N-terminal domain, a triple-helical domain in
the middle, and a globular noncollagenous (NC1) domain at the
C terminus. The biochemical properties of these structural compo-
nents are critical to understanding glomerular diseases. For exam-
ple, antigens in the NC1 domain are the targets of antibodies in
anti-GBM nephritis; genetic defects in the α-chains underlie some
forms of Alport syndrome; and the proteoglycan content of the
GBM may contribute to its permeability characteristics (Fig. 20.3).
•  The visceral epithelial cells (podocytes) form interdigitating pro-
cesses and are adherent to the lamina rara externa of the basement
membrane (see Fig. 20.1). Adjacent foot processes are separated by
20- to 30-nm–wide filtration slits, which are bridged by a unique
cell-cell junction, the slit diaphragm (see Fig. 20.2).
•  The entire glomerular tuft is supported by the mesangium, the tis-
sue that lies between the capillaries and is composed of basement
membrane–like mesangial matrix that forms a meshwork in which
the mesangial cells are embedded (see Fig. 20.1). These cells, of
mesenchymal origin, are contractile, phagocytic, and capable of
proliferation,  of  both  matrix  and  collagen  production,  and  of
secreting several biologically active mediators. Biologically, they are
most akin to vascular smooth muscle cells and pericytes. Because
no basement membrane separates mesangial cells from the capil-
lary loops, glomerulonephritides often affect both the mesangial
and the intracapillary compartments.
The normal glomerulus is highly permeable to water and small
solutes because of the fenestrated nature of the endothelium, and it
is impermeable to proteins of the size of albumin (,3.6-nm radius;
70 kilodaltons [kD] molecular weight) or larger. The permeability
characteristics of the glomerular filtration barrier allow discrimina-
tion among various protein molecules, depending on their size (the
larger, the less permeable) and charge (the more cationic, the more
permeable). This size- and charge-dependent barrier function is ac-
counted for by the structure of the capillary wall. The charge-depen-
dent restriction is important in the virtually complete exclusion of
albumin from the filtrate, because albumin is an anionic molecule.
The podocytes are important for the maintenance of glomerular bar-
rier function and are largely responsible, under normal circumstances, for
synthesis of GBM components. Their specialized junctional complex, the
slit diaphragm, represents a size-selective distal barrier to the filtration of
proteins,  enabling  effective  charge-  and  size-dependent  retention  of
plasma proteins. Proteins forming the slit diaphragm itself and mole-
cules that are part of the intracellular aspect of the slit diaphragm
complex are illustrated in Fig. 20.4. Nephrin is a transmembrane pro-
tein with a large extracellular portion composed of immunoglobulin
(Ig)-like domains. Nephrin molecules extend toward each other from
neighboring  foot  processes  and  dimerize  across  the  filtration  slit.
Within the cytoplasm of the foot processes, nephrin forms molecular
connections  with  intracellular  slit  diaphragm  components  such  as
podocin and CD2-associated protein (CD2AP), and ultimately links
with the actin cytoskeleton, which anchors on focal adhesion hubs.
The importance of the slit diaphragm proteins in maintaining glo-
merular barrier function is demonstrated by the observation that mu-
tations in the genes encoding them give rise to defects in permeability
and familial nephrotic syndromes (discussed later).
Pathologic Responses of the Glomerulus to Injury
Various types of glomerulopathies are characterized by one or more of
four basic tissue reactions.

Diseases Caused by In Situ Formation of Immune Complexes
In this form of injury, immune complexes are formed locally by anti-
bodies that react with intrinsic tissue antigens or with extrinsic anti-
gens “planted” in the glomerulus from the circulation (Fig. 20.5A).
Membranous nephropathy is the classic example of glomerular injury
resulting from local formation of immune complexes by antibodies
reactive with endogenous antigens. The target antigens are spatially
separated in the GBM and not continuous.
The pattern of deposition of antibodies and complement pro-
teins by immunofluorescence microscopy is granular, reflecting
localized accumulation of antigen-antibody complexes (Fig. 20.5D).
On electron microscopy, the glomerulopathy is characterized by the
presence of numerous discrete subepithelial electron-dense immune
complex  deposits.  These  subepithelial  deposits,  with  resultant
host responses, eventually result in a thickened basement membrane
appearance  by  light  microscopy;  hence  the  term  membranous
nephropathy.
Some antibodies that bind to intrinsic antigens directly interfere
with the function of glomerular proteins. An example are autoanti-
bodies described in minimal change disease, which bind to the slit
diaphragm component nephrin and disrupt the junctional complexes
between podocytes. These antibody-antigen complexes appear to be
short lived; as a result, they can be difficult to detect by immuno-
staining.
Antibodies can also react in situ with antigens that are not nor-
mally present in the glomerulus but are “planted” there. Such anti-
gens may localize to the kidney by interacting with various intrinsic
components of the glomerulus. Planted antigens include cationic mol-
ecules that bind to anionic components of the glomerulus; DNA, nu-
cleosomes, and other nuclear proteins, which may have an affinity for
GBM components; bacterial products; large aggregated proteins (e.g.,
aggregated immunoglobulins), which deposit in the mesangium due to
their size and biochemical properties; and immune complexes them-
selves, because they continue to have reactive sites for further interac-
tions with free antibody, free antigen, or complement. There is no
dearth of other possible planted antigens, including viral, bacterial, and
parasitic products and drugs.
Disease Caused by Antibodies Directed Against Normal
Components of the Glomerular Basement Membrane
In  anti-GBM  antibody–induced  glomerulonephritis,  antibodies
bind to intrinsic antigens distributed along the entire length of
the GBM, resulting in a diffuse linear pattern of staining for the
antibodies by immunofluorescence techniques (Fig. 20.5B,E). This
contrasts with the granular pattern of immunofluorescence staining
corresponding to the discrete immune complexes seen in membranous
nephropathy, or other glomerular diseases in which large complexes
of antigens and antibodies form in situ. Although anti-GBM antibody–
induced glomerulonephritis accounts for less than 5% of cases of human
glomerulonephritis, it is one of the more common causes of the clinical
syndrome of RPGN.
Glomerulonephritis Resulting From Deposition of Circulating
Immune Complexes
This type of glomerular injury is caused by the entrapment of circu-
lating antigen-antibody complexes within glomeruli. The antibodies
have no immunologic specificity for glomerular constituents, and the
complexes localize to the glomeruli because of their physicochemical

Electron  microscopy  reveals  electron-dense  deposits  containing
immune complexes that may lie in the mesangium, between the endo-
thelial cells and the GBM (subendothelial deposits), or between the
outer surface of the GBM and the podocytes (subepithelial deposits).
Deposits may be located at more than one site in a given case. By im-
munofluorescence microscopy, the immune complexes are seen as
granular deposits along the basement membrane (see Fig. 20.5D), in
the mesangium, or in both locations. Once deposited in the kidney,
immune complexes may eventually be degraded, mostly by infiltrating
neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages, mesangial cells, and endog-
enous proteases, and the inflammatory reaction may then subside,
allowing  for  complete  recovery  of  the  glomerulus.  Such  a  course
occurs when the exposure to the inciting antigen is short-lived and/or
limited,  as  in  most  cases  of  poststreptococcal  glomerulonephritis.
However, if immune complexes are deposited repeatedly for prolonged
periods, as may be seen with SLE or viral hepatitis, episodic cellular
injury and tissue remodeling results in membranous (subepithelial
deposition)  or  membranoproliferative  (subendothelial  deposition)
patterns of glomerular injury.
Several factors affect the localization of antigen, antibody, or im-
mune complexes in the glomerulus, such as the charge and size of the
immune  reactants,  glomerular  hemodynamics,  mesangial  function,
and the integrity of the charge-selective capillary wall barrier, leading to
variable patterns of immune-reactant deposition in various forms of
glomerulonephritis (Fig. 20.6). In turn, the distinct patterns of localiza-
tion of immune complexes are a key determinant of the injury response
and the histologic features that subsequently develop.
In  summary,  most  cases  of  immune  complex–mediated  glo-
merulonephritis are a consequence of deposition of discrete im-
mune complexes, which give rise to granular immunofluorescence
staining along the peripheral capillary wall or in the mesangium.
However, it is difficult to determine whether the deposition has oc-
curred  in  situ,  by  circulating  complexes,  or  by  both  mechanisms
because entrapment of circulating immune complexes can initiate
further in situ complex formation. Single etiologic agents, such as
hepatitis B and C viruses, can cause either a membranous pattern of
glomerulonephritis, with subepithelial in situ deposition of antigens,
or a membranoproliferative pattern indicative of subendothelial de-
position of antigens or deposition of circulating complexes.
Cell-Mediated Immunity in Glomerulonephritis
Although  antibody-mediated  mechanisms  initiate  most  forms  of
glomerulonephritis, there is evidence that sensitized T cells may also
cause glomerular injury and contribute to the progression of some glo-
merulonephritides. Clues to involvement of cellular immunity include
the presence of activated macrophages and T cells and their products in
the glomerulus in some forms of human and experimental glomerulo-
nephritis; in vitro and in vivo evidence of lymphocyte activation on
exposure to antigen in human and experimental glomerulonephritis;
abrogation of glomerular injury by lymphocyte depletion; and experi-
ments in which glomerular injury may be induced by transfer of T cells

both cells and molecules—are the usual suspects involved in acute and
chronic inflammation, described in Chapter 3, and only a few are
highlighted here.
Cells.  Numerous recruited and intrinsic cells produce mediators
that are responsible for glomerular injury.

glomerulonephritis, largely because of activation of complement,

which cause cell damage; and arachidonic acid metabolites, which
cause vascular changes that contribute to reductions in GFR.
•  Macrophages and T lymphocytes, which infiltrate glomeruli in
antibody- and cell-mediated reactions, release a vast number of
biologically active molecules when activated.

Cell-Mediated Immunity in Glomerulonephritis

Although  antibody-mediated  mechanisms  initiate  most  forms  of glomerulonephritis, there is evidence that sensitized T cells may also cause glomerular injury and contribute to the progression of some glomerulonephritides. Clues to involvement of cellular immunity include the presence of activated macrophages and T cells and their products in the glomerulus in some forms of human and experimental glomerulonephritis; in vitro and in vivo evidence of lymphocyte activation on exposure to antigen in human and experimental glomerulonephritis; abrogation of glomerular injury by lymphocyte depletion; and experiments in which glomerular injury may be induced by transfer of T cells

Activation of Alternative Complement Pathway

Alternative complement pathway activation occurs in the clinicopathologic entity called C3 glomerulopathy, which encompasses the entities of dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis. This is discussed later.
Mediators of Glomerular Injury

Once immune reactants or sensitized T cells have localized in the glomerulus, how does the glomerular damage ensue? The mediators— both cells and molecules—are the usual suspects involved in acute and chronic inflammation, described in Chapter 3, and only a few are highlighted here.
Cells.  Numerous recruited and intrinsic cells produce mediators that are responsible for glomerular injury.

•  Neutrophils and monocytes infiltrate glomeruli in certain types of glomerulonephritis, largely because of activation of complement, resulting in generation of chemotactic molecules (mainly C5a), but also by Fc receptor–mediated activation. Neutrophils release proteases, which cause GBM degradation; oxygen-derived free radicals, which cause cell damage; and arachidonic acid metabolites, which cause vascular changes that contribute to reductions in GFR.
•  Macrophages and T lymphocytes, which infiltrate glomeruli in antibody- and cell-mediated reactions, release a vast number of biologically active molecules when activated.

Mechanisms of Progression in Glomerular Diseases
Thus far, the immunologic mechanisms and mediators that initiate
glomerular injury have been discussed. The outcome of such injury
depends on several factors, including the severity of renal damage, the
nature and persistence of the antigens, and the immune status, age, and
genetic predisposition of the host.
It has long been known that once any renal disease, glomerular
or otherwise, destroys sufficient nephrons to reduce the GFR to
about 30% to 50% of normal, progression to end-stage kidney dis-
ease proceeds at a steady rate, independent of the original insult or
activity of the underlying disease. The secondary factors that lead to
progression are of great clinical interest because they are potential
targets of therapy that could delay or prevent the inexorable journey
to dialysis or transplantation.
The two major histologic characteristics of such progressive renal
damage are glomerulosclerosis and tubulointerstitial fibrosis.
Glomerulosclerosis.  Sclerosis involving portions of some glomer-
uli (also referred to as FSGS) develops after many types of renal injury
and can lead to proteinuria and increasing functional impairment.
Glomerulosclerosis may be seen even in cases in which the primary dis-
ease was nonglomerular. The mechanisms of glomerulosclerosis in this
setting are described in the discussion of FSGS later in this chapter.
Tubular Injury and Interstitial Fibrosis.  Tubulointerstitial injury,
manifested by tubular damage and interstitial inflammation, is a
component of many acute and chronic glomerulonephritides. Tu-
bulointerstitial fibrosis contributes to progression in both immune and
nonimmune glomerular diseases, for example, diabetic nephropathy.

•  Platelets may aggregate in glomeruli during immune-mediated injury.
Their release of eicosanoids, growth factors, and other mediators may contribute to vascular injury and proliferation of glomerular cells.
Antiplatelet agents have beneficial effects in both human and experimental glomerulonephritis.

•  Resident  glomerular  cells,  particularly  mesangial  cells,  can  be stimulated to produce inflammatory mediators, including reactive oxygen  species  (ROS),  cytokines,  chemokines,  growth  factors, eicosanoids, nitric oxide, and endothelin. They may initiate inflammatory responses in glomeruli, even in the absence of leukocytic infiltration.
Soluble Mediators.  Virtually all known inflammatory chemical mediators (Chapter 3) have been implicated in glomerular injury.

•  Complement  activation  leads  to  the  generation  of  chemotactic products that induce leukocyte influx (complement-neutrophil– dependent injury) and the formation of C5b–C9, the membrane attack complex. C5b–C9 causes cell lysis and may also stimulate mesangial cells to produce oxidants, proteases, and other mediators. Thus, even in the absence of neutrophils, C5b–C9 can cause proteinuria, as has been demonstrated in experimental membranous glomerulopathy. In some diseases, collectively called C3 glomerulopathies,  there  is  evidence  of  complement  activation resulting from defective regulation of the alternative complement pathway, which can be triggered or exacerbated by the presence of immune complexes or monoclonal immunoglobulins.
•  Eicosanoids, nitric oxide, angiotensin, and endothelin are involved in hemodynamic changes.

•  Cytokines,  particularly  IL-1  and  tumor  necrosis  factor  (TNF), which may be produced by infiltrating leukocytes and resident glomerular cells, induce leukocyte adhesion and a variety of other effects.

Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) maintains endothelial integrity and may help regulate capillary permeability.

Fibrin is frequently present in the glomeruli and Bowman space in glomerulonephritis, indicative of coagulation cascade activation, and activated coagulation factors, particularly thrombin, may be a stimulus for crescent formation.

KEY CONCEPTS
Pathogenesis of Glomerular Injury and Progression of
Glomerular Disease
•  Antibody-mediated injury is an important mechanism of glomerular dam-
age, mainly via complement- and leukocyte-mediated pathways. Antibodies
may also be directly cytotoxic to glomerular cells.
•  The  most  common  forms  of  antibody-mediated  glomerulonephritis  are
caused by the formation and accumulation of immune complexes, which may
involve either endogenous antigens (e.g., PLA₂R in membranous nephropa-
thy) or exogenous antigens (e.g., microbial). Immune complexes show a
granular pattern of deposition by immunofluorescence.
•  Binding of antibodies to intrinsic glomerular proteins can also directly lead
to glomerular dysfunction (e.g., nephrin in minimal change disease). In some
cases, immune complexes are small and short-lived and may not be readily
detectable by immunofluorescence.
•  Autoantibodies against components of the GBM are the cause of anti-
GBM antibody–mediated disease, often associated with severe injury.
The immunofluorescence pattern of antibody deposition is linear.
•  Activation of the alternative complement pathway is an important mechanism
of injury in C3 glomerulopathy that includes dense deposit disease and C3
glomerulonephritis.
•  Soluble inflammatory mediators, such as cytokines, chemokines, growth
factors, eicosanoids, nitric oxide, and activated coagulation factors, also
contribute to the glomerular injury.
•  Epithelial cell (podocyte) injury induced by antibodies, toxins, cytokines, infec-
tions, and poorly characterized circulating factors is a common manifestation
of various forms of glomerular diseases.
•  Progressive glomerular injury, resulting from either primary or secondary
causes, ensues from a cycle of glomerular and nephron loss with com-
pensatory changes, which lead to further glomerular injury, glomerulo-
sclerosis,  tubulointerstitial  fibrosis,  and  eventually  end-stage  kidney
disease.
Having discussed the factors involved in the initiation and progres-
sion of glomerular injury, we now turn to individual glomerular dis-
eases. Table 20.5 summarizes the main clinical and pathologic features
of the major forms of primary glomerulopathies.
Nephritic Syndrome
Glomerular  diseases  presenting  with  a  nephritic  syndrome  are
characterized by inflammation in the glomeruli. The main clinical
features of nephritic syndrome include:
•  Hematuria (red blood cells and red cell casts in urine)
•  Proteinuria (usually subnephrotic range) with or without edema

•  Azotemia
•  Hypertension
Nephritic syndrome is the typical clinical presentation of most
proliferative types of glomerulonephritis (GN) such as postinfec-
tious GN, rapidly progressive (crescentic) GN, and proliferative
lupus GN (described later, since it also causes nephrotic syndrome).
The lesions that cause the nephritic syndrome have in common
proliferation of the cells within the glomeruli, often accompanied
by infiltration of inflammatory leukocytes. This inflammatory re-
action severely injures the capillary walls, permitting blood to pass
into the urine and inducing hemodynamic changes that lead to a
reduction in GFR. The reduced GFR is manifested clinically by oli-
guria, fluid retention, and azotemia. Hypertension probably is a
result of both the fluid retention and renin release from the isch-
emic kidneys.
Acute Proliferative (Postinfectious and Infection-Associated)
Glomerulonephritis
Postinfectious GN is caused by deposition or formation of im-
mune  complexes  containing  microbial  antigens,  which  induce
infiltration of leukocytes and proliferation of glomerular cells.
The most common underlying infections are streptococcal, but the
disorder may also be associated with other infections. Poststrepto-
coccal GN is decreasing in frequency in the United States due to
early antibiotic treatment but continues to be a fairly common dis-
order worldwide. It usually appears 1 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal
infection of the pharynx or skin (impetigo). Skin infections are
commonly associated with overcrowding and poor hygiene. Post-
streptococcal glomerulonephritis occurs most frequently in chil-
dren 6 to 10 years of age, but children and adults of any age can be
affected.
Pathogenesis
Poststreptococcal GN is caused by immune complexes containing
streptococcal antigens and specific antibodies. Only certain strains
of group A β-hemolytic streptococci are nephritogenic, more than
90% of cases being traced to types 1, 4, and 12, which can be identified
by typing of the M protein of the bacterial cell walls.
Many lines of evidence support an immunologic basis for post-
streptococcal glomerulonephritis. The latent period between infection
and onset of nephritis is compatible with the time required for the
production of antibodies and the formation of immune complexes.
Elevated titers of antibodies against one or more streptococcal antigens
are present in a great majority of patients. Serum complement levels
are low, compatible with activation of the complement system and
consumption of complement components. There are granular immune
deposits in the glomeruli, indicative of an immune complex–mediated
mechanism.
The preponderance of evidence suggests streptococcal pyogenic
exotoxin B (SpeB) is the principal antigen in most but not all cases
of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. This protein is commonly
secreted by nephritogenic strains of streptococci, and has been lo-
calized to the “humplike” deposits characteristic of this disease
(described later). At the outset, the inciting antigens are exoge-
nously planted from the circulation in subendothelial locations in
glomerular capillary walls, leading to in situ formation of immune
complexes,  where  they  elicit  an  inflammatory  response.  Subse-
quently, through mechanisms that are not well understood, the
antigen-antibody complexes dissociate, migrate across the GBM,

interstitium, and reduced peritubular capillary blood supply. It appears that proteinuria can also cause direct injury to and activation of tubular cells. Activated tubular cells in turn express adhesion molecules and elaborate proinflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors that contribute to interstitial fibrosis. Filtered proteins that may produce these tubular effects include cytokines, complement products, the iron in hemoglobin, immunoglobulins, lipid moieties, and oxidized plasma proteins.

KEY CONCEPTS

Pathogenesis of Glomerular Injury and Progression of

Glomerular Disease

• Antibody-mediated injury is an important mechanism of glomerular damage, mainly via complement- and leukocyte-mediated pathways. Antibodies may also be directly cytotoxic to glomerular cells.

• The most common forms of antibody-mediated glomerulonephritis are caused by the formation and accumulation of immune complexes, which may involve either endogenous antigens (e.g., PLA₂R in membranous nephropathy) or exogenous antigens (e.g., microbial). Immune complexes show a granular pattern of deposition by immunofluorescence.

• Binding of antibodies to intrinsic glomerular proteins can also directly lead to glomerular dysfunction (e.g., nephrin in minimal change disease). In some cases, immune complexes are small and short-lived and may not be readily detectable by immunofluorescence.

• Autoantibodies against components of the GBM are the cause of anti- GBM antibody–mediated disease, often associated with severe injury.

The immunofluorescence pattern of antibody deposition is linear.

• Activation of the alternative complement pathway is an important mechanism of injury in C3 glomerulopathy that includes dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis.

• Soluble inflammatory mediators, such as cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, eicosanoids, nitric oxide, and activated coagulation factors, also contribute to the glomerular injury.

• Epithelial cell (podocyte) injury induced by antibodies, toxins, cytokines, infections, and poorly characterized circulating factors is a common manifestation of various forms of glomerular diseases.

• Progressive glomerular injury, resulting from either primary or secondary

causes, ensues from a cycle of glomerular and nephron loss with compensatory changes, which lead to further glomerular injury, glomerulosclerosis, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and eventually end-stage kidney

disease.

Having discussed the factors involved in the initiation and progression of glomerular injury, we now turn to individual glomerular diseases. Table 20.5 summarizes the main clinical and pathologic features

of the major forms of primary glomerulopathies.

Nephritic Syndrome

Glomerular diseases presenting with a nephritic syndrome are characterized by inflammation in the glomeruli. The main clinical features of nephritic syndrome include:

• Hematuria (red blood cells and red cell casts in urine)

• Proteinuria (usually subnephrotic range) with or without edema

• Azotemia

• Hypertension

Nephritic syndrome is the typical clinical presentation of most proliferative types of glomerulonephritis (GN) such as postinfectious GN, rapidly progressive (crescentic) GN, and proliferative lupus GN (described later, since it also causes nephrotic syndrome).

The lesions that cause the nephritic syndrome have in common proliferation of the cells within the glomeruli, often accompanied by infiltration of inflammatory leukocytes. This inflammatory reaction severely injures the capillary walls, permitting blood to pass into the urine and inducing hemodynamic changes that lead to a reduction in GFR. The reduced GFR is manifested clinically by oliguria, fluid retention, and azotemia. Hypertension probably is a result of both the fluid retention and renin release from the ischemic kidneys.

Acute Proliferative (Postinfectious and Infection-Associated) Glomerulonephritis

Postinfectious GN is caused by deposition or formation of immune complexes containing microbial antigens, which induce infiltration of leukocytes and proliferation of glomerular cells.

The most common underlying infections are streptococcal, but the disorder may also be associated with other infections. Poststreptococcal GN is decreasing in frequency in the United States due to early antibiotic treatment but continues to be a fairly common disorder worldwide. It usually appears 1 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal infection of the pharynx or skin (impetigo). Skin infections are commonly associated with overcrowding and poor hygiene. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis occurs most frequently in children 6 to 10 years of age, but children and adults of any age can be affected.

Pathogenesis

Poststreptococcal GN is caused by immune complexes containing streptococcal antigens and specific antibodies. Only certain strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci are nephritogenic, more than

90% of cases being traced to types 1, 4, and 12, which can be identified by typing of the M protein of the bacterial cell walls.

Elevated titers of antibodies against one or more streptococcal antigens are present in a great majority of patients. There are granular immune deposits in the glomeruli, indicative of an immune complex–mediated mechanism.

This protein is commonly secreted by nephritogenic strains of streptococci, and has been localized to the “humplike” deposits characteristic of this disease

(described later). CHAPTER 20 The Kidney 825
By immunofluorescence microscopy, there are granular deposits of IgG
and C3 (Fig. 20.8C), and sometimes IgM in the mesangium and along the GBM.
Although immune complex deposits are almost universally present, they are
often focal and sparse. The characteristic electron microscopic findings are
discrete, amorphous, electron-dense deposits on the epithelial side of the
membrane, often having the appearance of “humps” (Fig. 20.8D), presumably
representing the antigen-antibody complexes at the subepithelial cell surface.
Subendothelial deposits are also commonly seen, typically early in the disease
course, and mesangial and intramembranous deposits may be present.
Clinical Features
In the typical case, a young child abruptly develops malaise, fever,
nausea, oliguria, and hematuria (smoky or cola-colored urine) 1 to
2 weeks after recovery from a sore throat. The patients have dysmorphic red cells or red cell casts in the urine, mild proteinuria (usually
less than 1 g/day), periorbital edema, and mild to moderate hypertension. In adults the onset is more likely to be atypical, such as the
sudden appearance of hypertension or edema, frequently with elevation of BUN. The glomerulonephritis is subclinical in some infected
individuals, and is discovered only on screening for microscopic
hematuria carried out during epidemic outbreaks. Important laboratory findings include elevations of antistreptococcal antibody titers
and a decline in the serum concentration of C3 and other components
of the complement cascade.
More than 95% of affected children eventually recover renal function with conservative therapy aimed at maintaining sodium and water
balance. A small minority of children (perhaps less than 1%) do not
improve, become severely oliguric, and develop a rapidly progressive
form of glomerulonephritis (described later). Some of the remaining
patients undergo slow progression to chronic glomerulonephritis with
or without recurrence of an active nephritic picture. Prolonged and
persistent heavy proteinuria and abnormal GFR mark patients with an
unfavorable prognosis.
In adults, the disease is less benign. Although the overall prognosis
in epidemics is good, in only about 60% of sporadic cases do the
patients recover promptly. In the remainder, the glomerular lesions fail
to resolve quickly, as manifested by persistent proteinuria, hematuria,
and hypertension. In some of these patients, the lesions eventually
clear, but others develop chronic glomerulonephritis or even RPGN.

826 CHAPTER 20  The Kidney
by relatively rapid and progressive loss of renal function associated
with severe oliguria and signs of nephritic syndrome. The most com-
mon histologic picture is the presence of crescents in most of the
glomeruli, hence the name crescentic glomerulonephritis. As discussed
earlier, crescents are produced predominantly by the proliferation of
the epithelial cells lining the Bowman capsule. The presence of fibrous
(healed) crescents indicates that the injury has been present for some
time or is episodic; this presentation is often associated with slower
disease progression.
Pathogenesis
RPGN, typically associated with crescent formation, may be a manifes-
tation of several different diseases, some restricted to the kidney and
others systemic. Although no single mechanism can explain all cases,
there is little doubt that in most cases the glomerular injury is im-
munologically mediated. A practical classification divides crescentic
GN into several groups based on immunologic findings (Table 20.6),
which have been described as:
•  Anti-GBM  antibody–mediated  disease,  characterized  by  linear
deposits of IgG and, in many cases, C3 in the GBM. In some of these
patients,  the  anti-GBM  antibodies  cross-react  with  pulmonary
alveolar basement membranes to produce the clinical picture of
pulmonary hemorrhage associated with renal failure (Goodpasture
syndrome). Plasmapheresis to remove the pathogenic circulating
antibodies  is  the  mainstay  of  treatment,  which  also  includes
therapy to suppress the underlying immune response.
The antigen common to the alveoli and GBM is a peptide within
the noncollagenous portion of the a₃ chain of collagen type IV.
What triggers the formation of these autoantibodies is unclear.
Exposure to viruses or hydrocarbon solvents (found in paints and
dyes) has been implicated in some patients, as have various drugs
and cancers. There is a high prevalence of certain human leukocyte
antigen (HLA) alleles (e.g., HLA-DRB1) in affected patients, a find-
ing consistent with a genetic predisposition to autoimmunity.
•  Diseases caused by immune complex deposition, with granular deposits
of antibodies and complement by immunofluorescence. Crescentic GN
can be a complication of any of the immune complex nephritides,
including postinfectious glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, IgA
nephropathy,  fibrillary  GN  and  IgA  vasculitis/Henoch-Schönlein
purpura. These patients usually cannot be helped by plasmapheresis,
and they require treatment for the underlying disease.

alternative complement-regulatory pathway. While C3-related glomer-
ular disease is mostly associated with endocapillary proliferative or
membranoproliferative patterns of injury, it can rarely also present
with crescentic GN. Autoantibodies to complement-regulatory factors
or mutations in CFHR5, which encodes a putative complement regula-
tory protein, may be underlying causes. Ultrastructurally, glomeruli
often show ill-defined mildly electron-dense deposits with strong im-
munoreactivity for C3 by immunofluorescence.
•  Pauci-immune crescentic GN, defined by the lack of detectable anti-
GBM antibodies or a paucity of immune complexes by immunofluo-
rescence and electron microscopy. Most patients with this type of
crescentic GN have circulating antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibod-
ies (ANCAs) that produce a cytoplasmic (PR3-ANCA) or perinu-
clear (MPO-ANCA) staining pattern and are known to play a role in
some vasculitides (Chapter 11). This type of crescentic GN may be a
component of a systemic vasculitis such as granulomatosis with
polyangiitis (formerly called Wegener granulomatosis) or micro-

of proliferating epithelial cells and leukocytes within the Bowman capsule (periodic acid-Schiff stain). (B) Electron

(A, Courtesy Dr. MA Venkatachalam, University of Texas Health Sciences Center, San Antonio.)
Clinical Features
The renal manifestations of all forms of crescentic glomerulonephritis include hematuria with red blood cell casts in the urine, moderate proteinuria occasionally reaching the nephrotic range, and variable hypertension
and edema. In Goodpasture syndrome, the course may be dominated by
recurrent hemoptysis or even life-threatening pulmonary hemorrhage.
Measurement of serum anti-GBM antibodies, antinuclear antibodies and
ANCAs, and analysis of complement-regulatory factors are helpful in the
diagnosis of specific subtypes. Although milder forms of glomerular injury may subside, the renal involvement is usually progressive over a matter of weeks and culminates in severe oliguria. Recovery of renal function
may follow early intensive plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) combined
with steroids and cytotoxic agents in Goodpasture syndrome. This therapy
can reverse both pulmonary hemorrhage and renal failure. Other forms of
crescentic GN also respond well to steroids and cytotoxic agents. However,
despite therapy, many patients eventually require chronic dialysis or transplantation, particularly if the disease is discovered at a late stage.
KEY CONCEPTS
Nephritic Syndrome
• Nephritic syndrome is characterized by hematuria, oliguria with azotemia,
proteinuria, and hypertension.
• The most common causes are immunologically mediated glomerular injury;
lesions are characterized by proliferative changes and leukocyte infiltration.
• Acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis typically occurs after streptococcal infection in children and young adults but may occur following infection with
many other organisms; it is caused by deposition of immune complexes, mainly
in the subepithelial spaces, with abundant neutrophils and proliferation of glomerular cells. Most affected children recover; the prognosis is worse in adults.
• RPGN is a clinical entity with features of nephritic syndrome and rapid loss
of renal function.
• RPGN (commonly called crescentic GN) is associated with severe glomerular injury with fibrinoid necrosis, GBM breaks, and subsequent proliferation
of parietal epithelial cells forming crescents.
• Crescentic GN may be mediated by autoantibodies to the GBM or result
from immune complex deposition. It can also occur in the absence of significant antibody deposition; most patients with this type of crescentic GN
have ANCA-associated vasculitis with circulating ANCAs.
Nephrotic Syndrome
Certain glomerular diseases virtually always produce the nephrotic
syndrome. In addition, many other forms of primary and secondary
glomerulopathies discussed in this chapter may underlie the syndrome. Before the major diseases associated with nephrotic syndrome
are presented, the causes and pathophysiology of this clinical complex
are briefly discussed.
Pathophysiology
Nephrotic syndrome is caused by a derangement in glomerular capillary walls resulting in increased permeability to plasma proteins.
The manifestations of the syndrome include:
• Massive proteinuria, with the daily loss of 3.5 g or more of protein
(less in children)
• Hypoalbuminemia, with plasma albumin levels less than 3 g/dL
• Generalized edema
• Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria
The various components of nephrotic syndrome bear a logical relationship to one another. The glomerular capillary wall, composed of the
endothelium, GBM and podocytes, acts as a size and charge barrier
through which the plasma filtrate passes. Increased permeability resulting from either structural or physicochemical alterations in this barrier
allows proteins to escape from the plasma into the urinary space, resulting in proteinuria.
Heavy proteinuria depletes serum albumin levels at a rate beyond
the compensatory synthetic capacity of the liver, resulting in hypoalbuminemia. Increased renal catabolism of filtered albumin also contributes to hypoalbuminemia. The generalized edema is a direct
consequence of decreased intravascular colloid osmotic pressure because of low plasma albumin. There is also sodium and water retention, which aggravates the edema (Chapter 4). This seems to be due
to several factors, including compensatory secretion of aldosterone,
mediated by the hypovolemia-enhanced renin secretion; stimulation
of the sympathetic nervous system; and a reduction in the secretion
of natriuretic factors such as atrial natriuretic peptides. Edema is
characteristically soft and pitting, and is most marked in the periorbital regions and dependent portions of the body. If severe, hypoalbuminemia may also lead to pleural effusions and ascites.

The largest proportion of protein lost in the urine is albumin, but
globulins are also excreted in some diseases. The ratio of low to high
molecular weight proteins in the urine in various cases of nephrotic
syndrome is a manifestation of the selectivity of proteinuria. A highly
selective proteinuria consists mostly of low-molecular-weight proteins
(albumin, transferrin), whereas a poorly selective proteinuria consists
of higher-molecular-weight globulins in addition to albumin.
The genesis of hyperlipidemia is complex. Most patients with ne-
phrotic syndrome have increased blood levels of cholesterol, triglyceride,
very-low-density  lipoprotein,  low-density  lipoprotein,  lipoprotein(a),
and apoprotein, and there is a decrease in high-density lipoprotein
concentration in some patients. These alterations seem to be due to a
combination of increased synthesis of lipoproteins in the liver, abnormal
transport of circulating lipid particles, and decreased lipid catabolism.
Lipiduria follows hyperlipidemia, because lipoproteins also leak across
the glomerular capillary wall. The lipid appears in the urine either as free
fat or as oval fat bodies, representing lipoprotein resorbed by tubular
epithelial cells and then shed along with injured tubular cells that have
detached from the basement membrane.
Nephrotic patients are particularly vulnerable to infection, espe-
cially staphylococcal and pneumococcal infections, probably due to loss
of immunoglobulins in the urine. Thrombotic and thromboembolic
complications are also common in nephrotic syndrome, due in part to
loss of endogenous anticoagulants (e.g., antithrombin III) in the urine.
Renal vein thrombosis, once thought to be a cause of nephrotic syn-
drome, is most often a consequence of this hypercoagulable state, par-
ticularly in patients with membranous nephropathy (see later).

The  incidences  of  the  several  causes  of  nephrotic  syndrome  vary
according to age and geography. In children younger than 17 years in
North America, for example, nephrotic syndrome is almost always
caused by a lesion primary to the kidney; among adults, in contrast, it
is often associated with a systemic disease. Table 20.7 represents a com-
posite derived from several studies of the causes of nephrotic syndrome
TABLE 20.7  Causes of Nephrotic Syndrome

children, 60% in adults. Approximate prevalence of systemic disease 5 5% in
children, 40% in adults.
bMembranoproliferative and other proliferative glomerulonephritides may result
in mixed nephrotic/nephritic syndromes.
and is therefore only approximate. The most frequent systemic causes
of nephrotic syndrome are diabetes, amyloidosis, and SLE. The most
important of the primary glomerular lesions are minimal change dis-
ease, membranous nephropathy, and primary/idiopathic FSGS. The
first is most common in children in North America, the second is most
common in older adults, and primary FSGS occurs at all ages. These
three  lesions  are  discussed  individually  in  the  following  sections.
Other less common causes of nephrotic syndrome include the various
proliferative  glomerulonephritides  such  as  membranoproliferative
glomerulonephritis (MPGN) and IgA nephropathy.
Membranous Nephropathy
Membranous nephropathy is characterized by diffuse thickening of
the glomerular capillary wall due to the accumulation of antibody-
containing deposits along the subepithelial side of the basement
membrane. Approximately 75% of cases of membranous nephropathy
are considered primary. The remaining cases usually occur in associa-
tion with other systemic diseases, and hence are referred to as secondary
membranous nephropathy. The most notable of these associations are:
•  Drugs (penicillamine, captopril, gold, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory
drugs [NSAIDs]). From 1% to 7% of patients with rheumatoid arthri-
tis treated with penicillamine or gold (drugs now used infrequently
for this disease) develop membranous nephropathy.
•  Underlying malignant tumors, particularly carcinomas of the lung and
colon, and melanoma. According to some studies, these are present in
as many as 5% to 10% of adults with membranous nephropathy.
•  SLE. About 10% to 15% of glomerulonephritis in SLE is of the
membranous type.
•  Infections (chronic hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis, schistosomiasis,
malaria).
•  Other autoimmune disorders such as thyroiditis can be associated
with secondary membranous nephropathy.
Pathogenesis
Membranous nephropathy (MN) is a form of chronic immune com-
plex–mediated disease, in which the inciting antigens can sometimes
be identified in the immune complexes. The antigens may be endoge-
nous or exogenous. The endogenous antigens may be renal or nonrenal
(described  later).  Exogenous  antigens  include  those  derived  from
hepatitis B virus and Treponema pallidum in patients infected with
these microbes.
MN is caused in most cases by antibodies to a renal autoantigen. A
major advance came from the identification of the M-type phospholi-
pase A₂ receptor (PLA₂R) as the antigen that underlies ,60% of hu-
man MN. Autoantibody binding to PLA₂R, a membrane protein pres-
ent on the basal surface of glomerular epithelial cells, is followed by
complement activation and then shedding of the immune aggregates
from the cell surface to form characteristic deposits of immune com-
plexes along the subepithelial aspect of the basement membrane (see
Fig. 20.5C). Less often, the target antigens are neural epidermal growth
factor like 1 (NELL1), thrombospondin type-1 domain–containing 7A
(THSD7A), exostocin 1/2 (EXT1/2), neural cell adhesion molecule 1
(NCAM1)  or  neutral  endopeptidase  (CD10),  a  membrane  protein
recognized by placentally transferred maternal antibodies in cases of
neonatal membranous nephropathy. The identification of the most
common target antigens is of diagnostic and prognostic value, as as-
sociations with systemic autoimmune disease (exostosin) and malig-
nancy (e.g., NELL1) have been described.

nous nephropathy? There is a paucity of neutrophils, monocytes, or
platelets in glomeruli. The C5b-9 membrane attack complex of comple-
ment may be detected in lesions, but its role in pathogenesis is unclear.

immunoglobulin deposited in many cases of MN, PLA₂R-associated
MN in particular. How IgG4 may be associated with complement activa-
tion is not clear.
MORPHOLOGY
By light microscopy, the glomeruli either appear normal in the early stages of the
disease or exhibit uniform, diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary
wall (Fig. 20.10A). By electron microscopy, the thickening is seen to be caused by
irregular electron-dense deposits containing immune complexes between the
basement membrane and the overlying epithelial cells, with effacement of podo-
cyte foot processes (Fig. 20.10B and D). Basement membrane material is laid
down between these deposits by the podocytes, appearing as irregular spikes
protruding from the GBM. These spikes are best seen by silver stains, which color
the basement membrane, but not the deposits, black. In time, these spikes thicken
to produce domelike protrusions after the immune complex formation subsides
and eventually close over the immune deposits, burying them within a markedly
thickened, irregular membrane. Immunofluorescence microscopy demonstrates
that  the  granular  deposits  contain  both  immunoglobulins  and  complement
(Fig. 20.10C). Immunostains reveal presence of the relevant target antigens in the
deposits in most patients. As the disease advances, segmental sclerosis may oc-
cur and glomeruli may become totally sclerosed. The epithelial cells of the proxi-
mal tubules contain protein reabsorption droplets, and there may be considerable
interstitial mononuclear cell inflammation.
Clinical Features
This disorder usually presents with the insidious onset of nephrotic
syndrome or, in 15% of patients, with sub-nephrotic proteinuria. He-
maturia and mild hypertension are present in 15% to 35% of cases. It is
necessary in any patient to first rule out secondary causes of nephrotic
syndrome, because treatment of the underlying condition (malignant
neoplasm, infection, or SLE) or discontinuance of the offending drug
can reverse or ameliorate the injury.
The course of the disease is variable but generally indolent. In contrast
to minimal change disease, described later, the proteinuria is nonselective
and usually does not respond well to corticosteroid therapy. Complete or
partial remissions may occur in up to 40% of patients, even in some pa-
tients without therapy. Progression is associated with increasing sclerosis
of glomeruli, rising serum creatinine reflecting renal insufficiency, and
development of hypertension. Although proteinuria persists in more than
60% of patients, only about 10% die or progress to renal failure within
10 years, and no more than 40% eventually develop severe chronic kidney
disease or ESKD. The disease recurs in up to 40% of patients who un-
dergo transplantation for ESKD. Spontaneous remissions and a relatively
benign outcome occur more commonly in females and in those with
proteinuria in the subnephrotic range.
Because of the variable course of the disease, it has been difficult to
evaluate the overall effectiveness of corticosteroids or other immuno-
suppressive therapy in controlling the proteinuria or progression. B-cell
targeted therapeutics appear to be the most effective form of therapy to
date. It is thought that serologic typing of circulating antibodies to the
various antigens as biomarkers of disease activity may aid in the diag-
nosis, prognosis, and management of membranous nephropathy.
Minimal Change Disease (Diffuse Podocytopathy With
Minimal Changes)
This disorder is characterized by diffuse effacement of foot processes
of podocytes, detectable by electron microscopy, in glomeruli that
appear normal by light microscopy. It is the most frequent cause of
CHAPTER 20  The Kidney 829
nephrotic syndrome in children, but it is less common in adults (see
Table 20.7). The peak incidence is between 2 and 6 years of age. The
disease sometimes follows a respiratory infection or routine prophylactic
immunization.
Pathogenesis
Historically, this disease was characterized by absence of immune de-
posits in the glomerulus, which led to dismissal of antibody-mediated
causes. However, recent evidence points to an autoantibody-mediated
pathogenesis. The current hypothesis is that a subset of minimal change
disease is caused by circulating antibodies directed against nephrin, a
transmembrane podocyte protein and essential slit diaphragm compo-
nent, which cause podocyte injury through interference with nephrin
crosslinking. Proteinuria ensues due to the rapid breakdown of the
podocyte slit diaphragm accompanied by diffuse podocyte foot process
effacement, dramatically altering the permeability and selectivity of the
glomerular filter. The ultrastructural changes support a primary podo-
cyte injury (podocytopathy), and studies in animal models also suggest
the loss of glomerular polyanions. Thus, defects in the charge barrier
may contribute to the proteinuria.
MORPHOLOGY
The glomeruli are normal by light microscopy (Fig. 20.11A). By electron micros-
copy the GBM appears normal, and no electron-dense deposits are seen. The
principal lesion is in the podocytes, which show a uniform, diffuse
effacement of foot processes, along with loss of intervening slit dia-
phragms (Fig. 20.11B). This change, often incorrectly termed “fusion” of foot
processes, actually represents simplification of the epithelial cell architecture
with flattening, retraction, and swelling of foot processes, which is the result
of a collapse of their central actin cytoskeleton. Foot process effacement is
also present in other proteinuric states (e.g., membranous glomerulopathy,
diabetic nephropathy); however, it usually occurs at later stages of the disease
and in the context of significant architectural distortion of the glomerulus. It is
only when effacement is associated with normal glomeruli by light microscopy
that the diagnosis of minimal change disease can be made. In most patients,
these podocyte changes are completely reversible after corticosteroid therapy,
concomitant with remission of the proteinuria and disappearance of circulating
anti-nephrin antibodies. The cells of the proximal tubules are often laden with
lipid  and  protein,  reflecting  tubular  reabsorption  of  lipoproteins  passing
through diseased glomeruli (hence the historical name lipoid nephrosis for
this disease). Immunofluorescence studies can be negative, but often show
subtle diffuse, global fine granular staining for IgG over the podocytes, in the
absence of complement reactivity (Fig. 20.11C). IgG staining typically colocal-
izes with clustered nephrin and represents binding of anti-nephrin antibodies
in the tissue.
Clinical Features
Despite massive proteinuria, renal function most often remains stable,
and there is typically no hypertension or hematuria. The proteinuria usu-
ally is highly selective, most of the protein being albumin. A characteris-
tic feature is a dramatic response to corticosteroid therapy. Most chil-
dren  (.90%)  with  minimal  change  disease  respond  rapidly  to  this
treatment. However, proteinuria recurs in a significant proportion of pa-
tients, and the disease sometimes becomes steroid-dependent or -resis-
tant, and/or progresses to FSGS (discussed later). Nevertheless, the long-
term  prognosis  for  patients  is  excellent,  and  even  steroid-dependent
disease may resolve when children reach puberty. Although adults are
slower to respond, their long-term prognosis is also excellent. Steroid-
dependent and frequently relapsing disease has been reported to respond
well to B-cell depletion therapy.

Foot process effacement is also present in other proteinuric states (e.g., membranous glomerulopathy, diabetic nephropathy); however, it usually occurs at later stages of the disease and in the context of significant architectural distortion of the glomerulus. It is only when effacement is associated with normal glomeruli by light microscopy that the diagnosis of minimal change disease can be made. In most patients, these podocyte changes are completely reversible after corticosteroid therapy, concomitant with remission of the proteinuria and disappearance of circulating anti-nephrin antibodies. The cells of the proximal tubules are often laden with lipid and protein, reflecting tubular reabsorption of lipoproteins passing through diseased glomeruli (hence the historical name lipoid nephrosis for this disease). Immunofluorescence studies can be negative, but often show subtle diffuse, global fine granular staining for IgG over the podocytes, in the absence of complement reactivity (Fig. 20.11C). IgG staining typically colocal-izes with clustered nephrin and represents binding of anti-nephrin antibodies in the tissue.

Clinical Features

Despite massive proteinuria, renal function most often remains stable,

and there is typically no hypertension or hematuria. The proteinuria usually is highly selective, most of the protein being albumin. A characteristic feature is a dramatic response to corticosteroid therapy. Most children (>90%) with minimal change disease respond rapidly to this

treatment. However, proteinuria recurs in a significant proportion of patients, and the disease sometimes becomes steroid-dependent or -resistant, and/or progresses to FSGS (discussed later). Nevertheless, the long-term

prognosis for patients is excellent, and even steroid-dependent disease may resolve when children reach puberty. Although adults are slower to respond, their long-term prognosis is also excellent. Steroid-dependent and frequently relapsing disease has been reported to respond well to B-cell depletion therapy.

How IgG4 may be associated with complement activation is not clear.
MORPHOLOGY

By light microscopy, the glomeruli either appear normal in the early stages of the disease or exhibit uniform, diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall (Fig. 20.10A). By electron microscopy, the thickening is seen to be caused by irregular electron-dense deposits containing immune complexes between the basement membrane and the overlying epithelial cells, with effacement of podocyte foot processes (Fig. 20.10B and D). Basement membrane material is laid down between these deposits by the podocytes, appearing as irregular spikes protruding from the GBM. These spikes are best seen by silver stains, which color the basement membrane, but not the deposits, black. In time, these spikes thicken to produce domelike protrusions after the immune complex formation subsides and eventually close over the immune deposits, burying them within a markedly thickened, irregular membrane. Immunofluorescence microscopy demonstrates that  the  granular  deposits  contain  both  immunoglobulins  and  complement
(Fig. 20.10C). Immunostains reveal presence of the relevant target antigens in the

deposits in most patients. As the disease advances, segmental sclerosis may occur and glomeruli may become totally sclerosed. The epithelial cells of the proximal tubules contain protein reabsorption droplets, and there may be considerable
interstitial mononuclear cell inflammation.
Clinical Features

This disorder usually presents with the insidious onset of nephrotic syndrome or, in 15% of patients, with sub-nephrotic proteinuria. Hematuria and mild hypertension are present in 15% to 35% of cases. It is necessary in any patient to first rule out secondary causes of nephrotic syndrome, because treatment of the underlying condition (malignant neoplasm, infection, or SLE) or discontinuance of the offending drug can reverse or ameliorate the injury.

The course of the disease is variable but generally indolent. In contrast to minimal change disease, described later, the proteinuria is nonselective and usually does not respond well to corticosteroid therapy. Complete or partial remissions may occur in up to 40% of patients, even in some patients without therapy. Progression is associated with increasing sclerosis of glomeruli, rising serum creatinine reflecting renal insufficiency, and development of hypertension. Although proteinuria persists in more than
60% of patients, only about 10% die or progress to renal failure within

10 years, and no more than 40% eventually develop severe chronic kidney disease or ESKD. The disease recurs in up to 40% of patients who undergo transplantation for ESKD. Spontaneous remissions and a relatively benign outcome occur more commonly in females and in those with proteinuria in the subnephrotic range.

Because of the variable course of the disease, it has been difficult to evaluate the overall effectiveness of corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive therapy in controlling the proteinuria or progression. B-cell targeted therapeutics appear to be the most effective form of therapy to date. It is thought that serologic typing of circulating antibodies to the various antigens as biomarkers of disease activity may aid in the diagnosis, prognosis, and management of membranous nephropathy.
Minimal Change Disease (Diffuse Podocytopathy With
Minimal Changes)

This disorder is characterized by diffuse effacement of foot processes of podocytes, detectable by electron microscopy, in glomeruli that appear normal by light microscopy. It is the most frequent cause of

nephrotic syndrome in children, but it is less common in adults (see
Table 20.7). The peak incidence is between 2 and 6 years of age. The disease sometimes follows a respiratory infection or routine prophylactic immunization.
Pathogenesis

Historically, this disease was characterized by absence of immune deposits in the glomerulus, which led to dismissal of antibody-mediated causes. Proteinuria ensues due to the rapid breakdown of the podocyte slit diaphragm accompanied by diffuse podocyte foot process effacement, dramatically altering the permeability and selectivity of the glomerular filter. The ultrastructural changes support a primary podocyte injury (podocytopathy), and studies in animal models also suggest the loss of glomerular polyanions. Thus, defects in the charge barrier may contribute to the proteinuria.

Clinical Features

and there is typically no hypertension or hematuria. The proteinuria usually is highly selective, most of the protein being albumin. A characteristic feature is a dramatic response to corticosteroid therapy. Most children  (>90%)  with  minimal  change  disease  respond  rapidly  to  this

• Primary or idiopathic: A primary diffuse podocytopathy
• Viral infections and other toxic injuries: Podocyte loss in the setting
of viral infection (such as HIV, SARS-CoV-2), heroin addiction
(heroin nephropathy), sickle cell disease, or other forms of direct
toxic podocyte injury
• Adaptive changes: Podocyte damage due to the adaptive response to high
body mass index, loss of renal tissue (after nephrectomy, unilateral renal
agenesis, renal dysplasia, or reflux nephropathy), or in advanced
stages of any other renal disorder with significant nephron loss (most
commonly vascular disease)
• Inherited forms of FSGS, which are uncommon, are associated with
mutations in slit diaphragm– and actin cytoskeleton-associated
proteins
• High-risk APOL1 alleles: Following podocyte loss in patients carrying
certain APOL1 alleles
• Secondary: As a secondary event, reflecting scarring and nephron
dropout in cases of focal glomerulonephritis (e.g., IgA nephropathy, ANCA-associated vasculitis)
So-called idiopathic FSGS, a form of primary podocytopathy,
accounts for 10% and 35% of cases of nephrotic syndrome in children
and adults, respectively. The clinical signs differ from those of minimal
change disease in the following respects: (1) there is a higher incidence
of hematuria, reduced GFR, and hypertension; (2) proteinuria is more
often nonselective; (3) response to corticosteroid therapy is poor; and
(4) there is progression to chronic kidney disease, with at least 50% of
patients developing ESKD within 10 years.
Pathogenesis of Primary FSGS
Primary FSGS is marked by the same characteristic diffuse podocyte
injury that is seen in minimal change disease (diffuse podocytopathy).
However, in primary FSGS, the podocytopathy leads to a degree of
podocyte loss that exceeds the ability of the surviving podocytes to
compensate. The initiating mechanism likely involves undefined circulating factors and genetically determined defects affecting components
of the slit diaphragm. Once areas of the tuft are devoid of covering
podocytes, hyalinosis and sclerosis ensue, stemming from entrapment
of high molecular weight plasma proteins in hyperpermeable foci,
capillary collapse, and increased ECM deposition. The recurrence of
massive proteinuria after transplantation, sometimes within 24 hours,
with subsequent progression to overt lesions of FSGS, recapitulating
the disease in the native kidneys, points to persistence of the causative
circulating factor in some patients.
The discovery of a genetic basis for some cases of FSGS and other
causes of the nephrotic syndrome has improved the understanding of
the pathogenesis of proteinuria in the nephrotic syndrome and has
provided new methods for diagnosis and prognosis. Inherited forms of
FSGS may be associated with:
• The first relevant gene identified, NPHS1, encodes the protein
nephrin, a key component of the slit diaphragm (see Fig. 20.4).
Several mutations of the NPHS gene have been identified that give
rise to congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type, producing
a minimal change disease–like glomerulopathy with extensive foot
process effacement.
• A distinctive pattern of autosomal recessive FSGS results from
mutations in the NPHS2 gene, which encodes the intracellular slit
diaphragm associated protein podocin. Mutations in NPHS2 are one
cause of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome of childhood onset. Some
implicated podocin mutations are relatively common variants and
show incomplete penetrance; it is suspected that these variants may
increase susceptibility to forms of FSGS that are triggered by acquired
factors.
• Mutations in the gene encoding the podocyte actin-binding proteins α-actinin 4 (ACTN4) and inverted formin-2 (INF2) underlie
some cases of autosomal dominant FSGS, which can be insidious
in onset but have a high rate of progression to renal insufficiency.
• Mutations in the gene encoding TRPC6 have been found in some
families with adult-onset FSGS. This protein is widely expressed,
including in podocytes, and the pathogenic mutations may perturb
podocyte function by increasing calcium flux in these cells.
What the affected proteins have in common is their localization to
the slit diaphragm and to adjacent podocyte cytoskeletal structures.
Their specific functions and interactions are incompletely understood,
but they all contribute to the integrity of the glomerular filter.

FSGS in the Setting of Adaptive Changes.  Adaptive forms of FSGS
occur as a complication of glomerular and nonglomerular diseases lead-
ing to structural or functional reduction in renal tissue. Particularly
striking examples in which this occurs are reflux nephropathy and uni-
lateral renal agenesis. These may lead to progressive glomerulosclerosis
and renal failure. The glomerulosclerosis seems to be initiated by the
adaptive change that occurs in the relatively unaffected glomeruli of
diseased kidneys. Such a mechanism is suggested by experiments in rats
subjected to subtotal nephrectomy. Compensatory hypertrophy of the
remaining glomeruli initially maintains renal function in these animals,
but proteinuria and segmental glomerulosclerosis soon develop, eventu-
ally leading to diffuse global glomerulosclerosis and uremia. The glo-
merular hypertrophy is associated with hemodynamic changes, including
increases in glomerular blood flow, filtration, and transcapillary pressure
(glomerular hypertension), and often with systemic hypertension. A
similar mechanism underlies the development of hypertrophy and FSGS
in obese individuals with relative insufficiency of nephron mass com-
pared to body mass (obesity-related FSGS).
The sequence of events (Fig. 20.12) that is thought to lead to sclero-

leading to segments of GBM denuded of overlying foot processes and
consequent increased glomerular permeability to proteins similar to the
process seen in primary FSGS; and accumulation of proteins in the

Lipid droplets and foamy macrophages are often present (Fig. 20.13B). Glomeruli that do not show segmental lesions usually appear normal by light microscopy but may show increased mesangial matrix. By electron microscopy, both sclerotic and nonsclerotic areas show effacement of foot processes, which is diffuse in primary forms of FSGS during acute nephrotic syndrome, and there may also be focal detachment of the epithelial cells and denudation of the underlying GBM. By immunofluorescence microscopy, IgM and C3 may be present in the sclerotic areas and/or in the mesangium. In addition to the focal sclerosis, there may be pronounced hyalinosis and thickening of afferent arterioles, particularly in those forms associated with primary vascular injury. With progression of the disease, increased numbers of glomeruli become involved, and sclerosis spreads within each glomerulus as more podocytes are lost. In time, this leads to total (i.e., global) sclerosis of glomeruli, with pronounced tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis.

A morphologic variant of FSGS, called collapsing glomerulopathy, is characterized by retraction and/or collapse of the entire glomerular tuft, with or without additional FSGS lesions of the type described earlier (Fig. 20.14). This variant of FSGS is the result of accelerated and abundant podocyte loss, followed by capillary collapse and activation and proliferation of parietal epithelial cells, which will eventually migrate onto the denuded segment(s) of the tuft. Collapsing glomerulopathy can be seen in patients with high-risk APOL1 alleles, in those with vaso-occlusive disease and renal infarction, as a feature of drug-induced podocyte injury (e.g., pamidronate), and as the most characteristic lesion of HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN) and COVID-19-associated nephropathy (COVAN).
